title: The History of Vanilla — The Flavor That Shouldn't Exist
fullText: Every vanilla bean on every shelf in every grocery store on the planet was pollinated by a human hand. Not a machine, not a bee. A person using their fingertip and a tiny wooden stick pressing two microscopic parts of a flower together in a gesture that takes about 3 seconds. And that gesture repeated billions of times across the farms of Madagascar and Indonesia and Tahiti traces back to a single moment in 1841 when a 12-year-old boy on a tiny volcanic island in the Indian Ocean figured out what the greatest botonists in Europe could not. What nobody knew at the time was that this boy, born into slavery, orphaned at birth, would solve a puzzle that had frustrated scientists for 300 years. and he would never see a scent for it. But this story does not start with that boy. It starts with an orchid in a jungle and a love story told by the people who first gave vanilla to the world. Deep in the tropical lands along the Gulf Coast of Mexico in the region now called Veraracruz, a vine grows unlike any other plant in the Americas. It crawls up the trunks of tropical trees, sometimes reaching 30 m into the canopy with thick waxy leaves and pale green flowers that bloom for just a few hours before they wilt and die. This vine is vanilla plania. It belongs to the orchid family and it holds a distinction that no other orchid on earth can claim. It is the only orchid that produces an edible fruit. Those long, dark, slender pods you see in the spice aisle, the ones that smell like birthday cake and warmth and childhood, those are the fruit of this single species. And for thousands of years, only one group of people knew how to grow them. The Totten people of the Veraracruz coast were the first to cultivate vanilla, carefully tending to these orchid vines in their shaded tropical forests as far back as the 1200s. To the totenax, vanilla was not just a crop. It was sacred. They used it in temple rituals and as perfume, in medicine, and as a charm for good luck. They believed the plant was a gift from the gods. And they had a story to explain how it came to be. According to Totenac legend, a goddess princess named Zanat fell in love with a mortal man. Because the gods forbade their union, because a deity could not walk among men, Zanet transformed herself into a vanilla vine so that she could stay on earth. Every year, the vine would flower and produce fragrant fruit, a reminder of her love and sacrifice. The Totenac people treated the orchid with the reverence that story demanded. And for centuries, their relationship with vanilla remained quiet, local, and unknown to the wider world. This is where the story takes a turn nobody expected. In 1427, the Aztec Empire, expanding outward from its capital at Tenotitlan in the central highlands, conquered the Totenac people. The Aztecs quickly developed a taste for what they found growing in the Totenac lowlands. They called vanilla clixo kettle, which translates to black flour, a reference to the way the cured pods turn dark and shriveled. and they immediately found a use for it that would change vanilla's destiny forever. The Aztecs began mixing vanilla with cacao beans, ground corn, chili peppers, and honey to create a drink called exoc colatal. If that word sounds familiar, it should. This was the ancestor of hot chocolate. But zokalatal was nothing like the sweet milky drink you know today. It was bitter, spicy, frothy, and intense. The Aztecs believed it gave strength, cured fatigue and contained divine nectar, and it was not for everyone. Zokalatal was reserved strictly for royalty, priests, and elite warriors. Common people never tasted it. Vanilla in its very first chapter outside the Tutonak homeland was already a luxury. The Aztecs forced the Totenac people to grow vanilla as tribute, essentially a tax paid in spice to the Aztec king. Year after year, the Totenacs harvested their sacred vine and sent the cured pods up to the Highland capital. Vanilla was not just valuable, it was a form of currency. And the Aztec Emperor Montazuma was, by all accounts, obsessed with it. Historical records suggest he drank dozens of cups of Zocalatal every day, flavored with vanilla from Golden Goblets. Pay attention to this next detail because it explains everything that followed. In 1519, the Spanish concistador Ernnan Cortez sailed from Spain to the coast of Mexico. He landed near what is now Veraracruz, the very heartland of Vanilla and marched inland toward the Aztec capital. When Cortez arrived in Tennochitlan, Montazuma greeted him with ceremony and hospitality, possibly believing Cortez was the returning god, Ketzal Kawatal. Among the offerings Montazuma presented was a golden goblet of Zakalatal, the chocolate and vanilla drink that had fueled the Aztec elite for generations. Cortez was reportedly stunned by the flavor. He had never encountered anything like it. The Spanish took careful note of both ingredients, the cacao and this mysterious dark pod that gave the drink its intoxicating aroma. They named the spice vineya, a Spanish word meaning little sheath, a reference to the pod's shape. And when Cortez returned to Spain, he brought vanilla with him. Within decades, vanilla had reached the royal courts of Europe. At first, the Spanish tried to keep vanilla a secret, hoarding the supply and mixing it exclusively with chocolate for the royal household. But secrets like that do not last. By the late 1500s, vanilla had spread across the continent. Queen Elizabeth I 1 of England reportedly became so fond of vanilla that she demanded it be added to her desserts without chocolate, making her one of the first Europeans on record to appreciate vanilla as a standalone flavor rather than a chocolate companion. In France, the aristocracy treated it as a prized ingredient for perfumes, pastries, and elaborate confections. Apothecries in Paris prescribed vanilla as a remedy for everything from headaches to impotence, which whether or not it worked, certainly helped drive demand. Vanilla quickly became a symbol of wealth and refinement across Europe. The pods were so expensive that only the very rich could afford them. A single vanilla bean in 17th century Europe could cost as much as a week's wages for a laborer, and that exclusivity only added to its appeal. The French court under Louis I 14th consumed vanilla in enormous quantities flavoring ice creams, custards and the elaborate multicourse desserts that defined aristocratic dining. Centuries later, Thomas Jefferson after spending 5 years in Paris as the American minister to France became so taken with vanilla that he wrote down one of the first known American ice cream recipes featuring a stick of vanilla. In 1791, already back in the United States and serving as Secretary of State, he ordered 50 vanilla bean pods shipped to him from France, writing that they were much used in seasoning ice creams. He later served vanilla ice cream at the White House during his presidency, and guests wrote home in amazement about the frozen dessert. Jefferson did not invent vanilla ice cream, but he may have done more than anyone else to popularize it in America. Vanilla had conquered the taste buds of the western world. Demand was exploding and there was a problem. A very big, very strange, very stubborn problem. The vanilla orchid refused to grow outside of Mexico. For 300 years, from the 1500s through the 1800s, European colonial powers tried to cultivate vanilla in their tropical territories. They shipped cutings to botanical gardens in Paris and London. They planted vanilla vines on islands across the Indian Ocean, in the Caribbean, in Southeast Asia. The vines grew beautifully. The leaves were green and thick. The flowers bloomed right on schedule. And then nothing. The orchid would flower, the petals would drop, and no pod would form ever. Imagine the frustration. Hundreds of botonists, decades of effort, entire colonial agricultural programs dedicated to cracking this mystery, and every single attempt failed. The vines produced gorgeous flowers, but not a single vanilla bean outside of Mexican soil. For a while, things actually seemed fine for the Europeans. They could just import vanilla from Mexico at enormous cost and sell it to the wealthy. That arrangement held, but the price was staggering. Vanilla was one of the most expensive spices in the world and the supply was limited to whatever the Mexican farmers could produce. The colonial powers wanted their own supply. They needed to grow vanilla themselves and the plant would not cooperate. Here is the detail that everyone missed at the time. The problem was not the soil. It was not the climate. It was not the water or the sunlight or the altitude. It was a bee. One specific bee, the melona bee. A small stingless species native to Central America and Mexico was the only insect capable of pollinating the vanilla orchid. The vanilla flower has a unique anatomy. It contains both male and female parts, but a thin membrane called the rosttolum separates them preventing the flower from pollinating itself. The melopona bee, small enough and persistent enough to navigate this barrier, was the only creature that could push past the rostellum and bring the pollen into contact with the stigma. And that was only part of the challenge. Each vanilla flower blooms for a single day. In some accounts, the window is even shorter, just a few hours in the morning before the flower wilts and closes forever. If a melopona bee does not visit during those few hours, that flower will never produce a pod one day, a few hours, one specific bee. That is why vanilla existed only in Mexico. The melipona bee did not live anywhere else on Earth. I mean, think about that for a second. The entire global vanilla supply from the 1500s to the 1800s depended on whether a tiny stingless bee in a Mexican jungle happened to visit the right flower on the right morning. In 1836, a Belgian botonist named Charles Morren published a paper describing an artificial pollination method for vanilla. He had figured out in theory how to do what the bee did, but his technique was fiddly and slow. better suited for a greenhouse experiment than a working plantation. It was not practical for any kind of large-scale cultivation. The mystery remained effectively unsolved. Everything was in place for a breakthrough. The scientific community just did not know what that breakthrough was building toward. And then we arrive at Reunion Island 1841. Reunion, then known as Bourban Island, is a small volcanic island in the Indian Ocean about 900 km east of Madagascar. French colonists had brought vanilla cutings to the island in the 1820s, hoping to start commercial production. The vines grew, the flowers bloomed, and just like everywhere else outside Mexico, no fruit appeared. The vines sat barren for 20 years. On a plantation in the town of St. Suzanne, a man named Fel Belellier Bowmont tended his gardens. Bellier Bowmont was a colonist and enslaver and among the people he enslaved was a boy named Edmund. Edmund had been born on the island around 1829. His mother, an enslaved woman, died during childbirth. He never knew his father. Belellier Bowmont took a particular interest in the boy and taught him about plants, about bot, about how flowers reproduced. He showed Edmund how to cross-pollinate other crops like watermelons and pumpkins by hand. One day in 1841, Belellier Bowmont was walking through his gardens with 12-year-old Edmund when he noticed something that stopped him cold. Two green vanilla pods were hanging from a vine. A vine that had been barren for 20 years, a vine that had never produced a single bean. Belellier Bowmont could not believe it. He asked Edmund if he knew anything about it. Edmund told him that he had done it himself. At first, Bellier Bowmont did not believe that a 12-year-old boy had accomplished what the greatest botonists in Europe had failed to do for three centuries. A few days later, more pods appeared on the vine. Belellier Bowmont asked Edmund to demonstrate his technique. What Edmund showed him was breathtakingly simple and impossibly clever at the same time. He took a thin wooden splinter, a small stick no bigger than a toothpick, and approached a freshly opened vanilla flower. With one hand, he steadied the blossom. With the splinter, he gently lifted the rostellum, that tiny membrane separating the male and female parts of the flower. Then, with his thumb, he pressed the pollen mass firmly against the stigma, completing the pollination in a matter of seconds. The whole procedure took no more than 2 or 3 seconds per flower. It required no special tools, no equipment, no laboratory, just a steady hand, a thin stick, and the knowledge of exactly which flap to lift. The technique was likely inspired by what Bellier Bowmont had taught him about cross-pollinating other plants like watermelons and pumpkins. Edmund had taken that knowledge and applied it to the vanilla orchid, something nobody in the scientific world had thought to try. As one historian later put it, Edmund's invention appears disarmingly simple, but only after the fact. Before Edmund, the finest minds in European bot had stared at the same flower and seen nothing but failure. This 12-year-old boy born into slavery, orphaned at birth with no formal education, had cracked the 300-year-old mystery of vanilla. Belellier Bowmont immediately spread the technique across Reunion Island. Within months, vanilla production on the island exploded. Within a few years, the method had been taught to farmers on Madagascar, the Comos Islands, and eventually across every tropical region where vanilla vines grew. For the first time in history, vanilla could be cultivated commercially outside of Mexico. But this is where the story stopped being uplifting, which looking back was maybe inevitable given the circumstances. A French botonist named Jean Michelle Claude Richard came forward and claimed that he had actually developed the same hand pollination method years earlier and that Edmund must have seen his demonstration and simply copied it. Bellier Bowmont pushed back hard. He defended Edmund and pointed out that the timelines made Richard's claim impossible. Modern historians have thoroughly examined the evidence and concluded that there is absolutely no reason to doubt that Edmund figured out the technique on his own. He had been trained in cross-pollination of other plants. He applied that knowledge to a flower nobody else thought to try it on. It was his discovery. Slavery was abolished on Reunion Island in 1848. Edmund was freed and given the surname Albus, but freedom did not bring prosperity. Edmund Albus struggled for the rest of his life. He was convicted of a minor theft at one point and sentenced to prison. Though Belellier Bowmont successfully petitioned for his early release, Edmund never received any compensation, any recognition, any financial reward for a technique that had unlocked a global industry. On August 9th, 1880, Edmund Albus died in a public hospital in St. Suzanne at the age of 51. A local newspaper noted his passing with a single devastating observation. The very man who at great profit to this colony discovered how to pollinate vanilla flowers has died in the public hospital. It was a destitute and miserable end. And somehow it gets worse when you zoom out from Edmund's personal story and look at what his technique created. The handpollination method spread from reunion to Madagascar in the 1850s and 1860s and Madagascar's northeastern coast turned out to be paradise for vanilla orchids. The Sava region encompassing the towns of Sambba, Antala, Vheima, and Andapa had the perfect combination of tropical heat, humidity, and rainfall. By the late 1800s, Madagascar had become the dominant vanilla producer on the planet. Today, that single island nation produces roughly 80% of the world's bourbon vanilla supply. Roughly 70,000 smallh holder farmers in the Sava region grow vanilla on plots smaller than a hectare tending the vines by hand just as the Totenacs did centuries ago in Mexico. And here is the part that connects everything. Every single one of those farmers every morning during pollination season, walks through their vanilla orchards at dawn, inspects each vine for freshly opened flowers, and performs the exact technique that Edmund Albus invented in 1841. The same gesture, the same thin stick, the same 3-second motion. Nearly two centuries later, on farms halfway around the world from where Edmund lived. His discovery is performed millions of times each season. It has never been improved upon. It has never been mechanized. It has never been replaced. But vanilla's story did not end with Edmund. Because while farmers on Madagascar were perfecting the art of hand pollination, chemists in Europe were working on something entirely different. In 1874, two German scientists named Ferdinand Teeman and Wilhelm Harmon figured out how to synthesize vanilla, the primary flavor compound in vanilla beans from coniferin, a substance found in pine bark. They filed a patent, founded a factory in Holtzmind, Germany, and began the first industrial production of a synthetic aroma chemical in history. Two years later, another chemist named Carl Rhymer synthesized vanoline from guacol. By the late 1800s, semiynthetic vanoline derived from clove oil was commercially available. The significance of this cannot be overstated. Natural vanilla beans contain over 250 individual flavor compounds that together create the complex, rich taste profile we associate with real vanilla. But vanoline is the dominant molecule, the one your brain recognizes as vanilla. Synthetic vanoline replicates that single molecule cheaply and at scale. It does not capture the full 250 compound symphony of a real bean. But for most commercial applications, from ice cream to cookies to candles, it is close enough. By the 1930s, synthetic vanoline production had shifted to lignen, a waste product from paper mills. And then in the 1970s, the prochemical root took over. Today, over 85% of all vanilla flavoring consumed worldwide is synthetic vanilla, most of it derived from prochemical precursors. The global synthetic vanoline market produces around 20,000 tons per year. Natural vanilla beans, by comparison, contribute fewer than 40 tons of actual vanoline to the world's supply. If you have ever eaten anything vanilla flavored that did not specifically say natural vanilla extract, you almost certainly ate a prochemical derivative. And no, that is not necessarily a bad thing. Blind taste tests have shown that most people cannot reliably distinguish between synthetic and natural vanilla in baked goods, where the heat breaks down many of the subtler compounds. Anyway, in a cookie or a cake, the difference between a $5 bottle of imitation vanilla and a $30 bottle of pure extract is negligible for most pallets. Synthetic vanilla made vanilla flavor accessible to billions of people who could never have afforded the real thing. It democratized a taste that had been reserved for royalty for centuries. The kid eating vanilla pudding from a plastic cup at a school cafeteria in Ohio is experiencing a flavor that Aztec emperors once restricted to the elite. That is not nothing. But there is a real difference in applications where vanilla is the star rather than a supporting player. In high-end ice cream, in creme brulee, in perfume, the full complexity of natural vanilla beans with their hints of caramel and smoke and dried fruit, their slightly boozy warmth is irreplaceable. This is why the market for real vanilla beans has never disappeared. Even as synthetic vanilla dominates the industry, some flavors can be replicated, others can only be approximated. But real vanilla endured and the economics of that survival are among the wildest in any agricultural commodity on Earth. Vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world, right behind saffron, and its price is staggeringly volatile. In the early 2000s, Madagascar vanilla beans sold for around 20 to $30 per kilogram. Then in 2000, cyclone Huda flattened the northeastern growing region. Because it takes three full years for a newly planted vanilla orchid to produce its first flowers, harvests dropped sharply and prices spiked to over $400 per kilogram. By 2003, nearly 30% of vanilla buyers switched to synthetic alternatives. Prices eventually crashed. Then they surged again. By 2018, vanilla beans hit over $500 per kilogram. At that price point, vanilla was nearly as expensive as silver by weight. If you are wondering how that is even possible for a plant, so is everyone else. The volatility has real human consequences. When prices are high, vanilla becomes a target for theft. Farmers in Madagascar have been attacked and killed for their vanilla crops. Some farmers began sleeping in their fields to guard the vines. Others started harvesting their beans early before the pods had fully matured just to prevent them from being stolen. Early harvesting means inferior flavor, which means lower quality beans flooding the market, which means the reputation of Madagascar vanilla suffers, which drives some buyers towards synthetic alternatives, which eventually crashes the price again. It is a vicious cycle and the farmers at the bottom of the supply chain absorb most of the pain. And through all of this, the fundamental process has not changed. The vanilla orchid still takes 3 to 4 years to mature before its first flower. Each flower still opens for a single day. Each flower still must be pollinated by hand using a thin stick and a thumbnail. After pollination, the green pods take 7 to 9 months to mature on the vine, and then the curing process begins. Curing vanilla is an art form unto itself, closer to wine- making or fermentation than anything you would normally associate with growing a spice. The green pods are first killed, which is the actual term used, by briefly blanching them in hot water at around 65° C. Then they are wrapped in dark cloth and placed in wooden boxes to sweat. Over the next several weeks, they are laid out in the tropical sun during the day and carefully packed away each night. A daily ritual that slowly draws out moisture, darkens the pods from green to deep brown, and triggers the enzyatic reactions that break down the flavorless precursor compounds into vanilla and the other 200 plus molecules that give real vanilla its depth. The full curing process takes 6 to9 months. Roughly 6 to 8 kg of green vanilla beans are needed to produce a single kilogram of the finished export ready product. From the moment a farmer pollinates a flower to the moment a cured vanilla bean reaches a store shelf, more than a year has passed. Every step done by hand. So when people use the word vanilla to mean plain, boring or ordinary, they are accidentally using one of the most ironic expressions in the English language. There is nothing plain about vanilla. It comes from the only edible orchid fruit on Earth. It was sacred to an ancient civilization and stolen by an empire. It stumped the finest scientific minds in Europe for three centuries. Its commercial existence depends on a technique invented by an enslaved child who died in poverty. It is grown by tens of thousands of farmers using methods unchanged since the 1800s. It is pollinated by hand, one flower at a time in a window of a few hours, once a year. It is cured for months in a process closer to wine- making than agriculture. And it remains one of the most volatile, contested, and laborintensive crops on the planet. Vanilla is not boring. Vanilla is one of the most extraordinary flavors that has ever existed. And the fact that it exists at all, that it survived the collapse of the Totenac civilization, the greed of empires, the cruelty of slavery, the rise of synthetic chemistry, and the chaos of global commodity markets is not something we should take for granted. The next time you taste vanilla in ice cream, in coffee, in a candle burning on your kitchen table, remember that what you are experiencing is the end result of a chain of events stretching back a thousand years, passing through jungles and laboratories and slave plantations and volcanic islands. And at the center of that chain, a 12-year-old boy with a thin wooden stick pressing two tiny parts of a flower together and changing the world in 3 seconds flat. What endures from vanilla's story is not just a flavor. It is Edmund Albus whose name should be famous but is not. It is the 70,000 farmers on Madagascar who still wake before dawn to pollinate flowers by hand. And it is the orchid itself, fragile and stubborn and impossible. Still blooming one day a year, still demanding that someone show up in time. fullTextVi: Mỗi hạt vani trên mỗi kệ ở mọi cửa hàng tạp hóa trên hành tinh đều là được thụ phấn bởi bàn tay con người. Không phải máy móc, không phải con ong. Một người dùng đầu ngón tay và một thanh gỗ nhỏ ấn vào hai bộ phận cực nhỏ của một bông hoa với nhau trong một cử chỉ mất khoảng 3 giây. Và cử chỉ đó được lặp lại hàng tỷ lần trên khắp các trang trại ở Madagascar và Indonesia và Tahiti quay lại một khoảnh khắc vào năm 1841 khi một cậu bé 12 tuổi trên một hòn đảo núi lửa nhỏ bé ở Ấn Độ Dương đã tìm ra điều gì vĩ đại nhất các nhà thực vật học ở châu Âu không thể làm được. Điều mà không ai biết vào thời điểm đó là cậu bé này sinh ra trong cảnh nô lệ, mồ côi khi sinh ra sẽ giải được một câu đố khiến các nhà khoa học thất vọng suốt 300 năm. và anh ấy sẽ không bao giờ nhìn thấy mùi hương của nó. Nhưng câu chuyện này không bắt đầu từ cậu bé đó. Nó bắt đầu với một bông lan trong rừng và một câu chuyện tình yêu được kể bởi những người đầu tiên mang hương vani đến với thế giới. Sâu trong vùng đất nhiệt đới dọc theo Bờ Vịnh Mexico trong khu vực bây giờ được gọi là Veraracruz, một loại cây nho mọc không giống bất kỳ loại cây nào khác ở Châu Mỹ. Nó bò lên thân cây nhiệt đới, có khi đạt tới 30 m vào tán với những chiếc lá sáp dày và những bông hoa màu xanh nhạt nở chỉ trong một vài giờ trước khi chúng héo và chết. Cây nho này là vani plania. Nó thuộc họ lan và nó có một nét khác biệt không có loài nào khác phong lan trên trái đất có thể yêu cầu. Đây là loài lan duy nhất có quả ăn được. Những quả dài, sẫm màu, mảnh mai mà bạn nhìn thấy ở quầy bán gia vị, những quả mùi như bánh sinh nhật, sự ấm áp và tuổi thơ, đó là thành quả của điều này loài đơn lẻ. Và suốt hàng ngàn năm qua, chỉ có một nhóm người biết cách trưởng thành them. Người Totten ở bờ biển Veracruz là những người đầu tiên trồng vani một cách cẩn thận chăm sóc những cây lan này trong những khu rừng nhiệt đới râm mát xa xưa những năm 1200. Đối với totenax, vani không chỉ là một loại cây trồng. Nó thật thiêng liêng. Họ sử dụng nó trong các nghi lễ đền thờ, làm nước hoa, trong y học và làm bùa may mắn. Họ tin rằng loài cây này là một món quà từ các vị thần. Và họ có một câu chuyện để giải thích nó diễn ra như thế nào. Theo truyền thuyết Totenac, một nữ thần công chúa tên là Zanat đã yêu một kẻ phàm trần. Bởi vì các vị thần cấm họ kết hợp, bởi vì một vị thần không thể bước đi giữa con người, Zanet biến mình thành cây nho vani để có thể ở lại trái đất. Hàng năm cây nho lại ra hoa và cho quả thơm, nhắc nhở về cô tình yêu và sự hy sinh. Người Totenac đối xử với cây lan bằng sự tôn kính mà câu chuyện yêu cầu. Và trong nhiều thế kỷ, mối quan hệ của họ với vani vẫn lặng lẽ, mang tính địa phương và không được biết đến. thế giới rộng lớn hơn. Đây là nơi câu chuyện rẽ sang một hướng không ai mong đợi. Năm 1427, Đế quốc Aztec mở rộng ra ngoài thủ đô Tenotitlan ở Tây Nguyên, chinh phục người Totenac. Người Aztec nhanh chóng phát triển sở thích về những thứ họ tìm thấy đang phát triển ở Totenac vùng đất thấp. Họ gọi ấm đun nước vani clixo, có nghĩa là bột mì đen, ám chỉ cách vỏ quả được chữa khỏi trở nên sẫm màu và teo lại. và họ ngay lập tức tìm ra cách sử dụng nó để thay đổi vận mệnh của vanilla mãi mãi. Người Aztec bắt đầu trộn vani với hạt cacao, ngô xay, ớt và mật ong để tạo ra một loại đồ uống gọi là exoc colatal. Nếu từ đó nghe có vẻ quen thuộc thì nó nên như vậy. Đây là tổ tiên của sôcôla nóng. Nhưng zokalatal không giống đồ uống ngọt ngào như sữa mà bạn biết ngày nay. Nó đắng, cay, sủi bọt và mãnh liệt. Người Aztec tin rằng nó mang lại sức mạnh, chữa khỏi mệt mỏi và chứa mật hoa thần thánh, và nó không dành cho tất cả mọi người. Zokalalal được dành riêng cho hoàng gia, linh mục và chiến binh ưu tú. Người bình thường chưa bao giờ nếm thử nó. Vani ngay từ chương đầu tiên bên ngoài quê hương Tutonak đã là một thứ xa xỉ.
